title: Inhibit System Recovery
summary: Inhibiting system recovery is the removal or disablement of the mechanisms that would let an organisation restore systems and data after destructive activity. It is the step that converts a recoverable outage into an existential one, and it is usually executed shortly before or alongside mass encryption or wiping activity. The mechanism targets every layer of resilience. On endpoints and file servers, native utilities that manage volume shadow copies and system restore points can delete recovery data, and boot configuration or recovery partitions can be modified so that built in repair options no longer work. Backup catalogues, backup files and backup agents can be deleted, stopped or reconfigured to point at storage that has been wiped, and backup infrastructure is often attacked directly because it holds credentials and trust relationships for everything else. In virtualised environments, hypervisor snapshots and datastores are removed. In cloud environments, snapshot deletion, backup vault tampering, retention policy changes and lifecycle rule manipulation achieve the same result through authenticated control plane calls. The telemetry is administrative and therefore easy to overlook. Endpoint and file server logs show shadow copy, restore point and backup service operations, often with the calling process, account and command line. Backup product audit logs record job deletion, catalogue changes and retention edits, and a sudden drop in successful backup jobs is itself a signal. Hypervisor and cloud audit logs record snapshot and vault operations together with the caller principal. Investigators distinguish malicious recovery inhibition from routine operations by correlating it with encryption, credential access and defence evasion in the same window, by checking whether the operation was scoped far more broadly than normal, by examining the account that performed it and whether that account was recently created or compromised, and by confirming the absence of a change record. Legitimate backup rotation and storage reclamation follow schedules and retain older copies, whereas malicious removal tends to be comprehensive and immediate. Monitoring that treats backup and snapshot deletion as high severity events in their own right is the most reliable control.
objectives: Explain how recovery inhibition targets endpoint, backup, hypervisor and cloud layers of resilience.
Identify the administrative artefacts that reveal shadow copy, snapshot, backup job and retention policy tampering.
Treat sudden degradation in backup success rates and catalogue integrity as a detection signal.
Differentiate scheduled backup rotation and storage reclamation from comprehensive malicious removal.
Correlate recovery inhibition with concurrent encryption, credential access and defence evasion activity.
Recommend monitoring, immutability and out of band recovery design that keeps restoration possible during an incident.

beginner.definition: This technique is about destroying the ways you would normally recover. The attacker deletes backups, snapshots and restore points, or turns the recovery tools off. It usually happens just before or during encryption, and it is what turns a bad day into an unrecoverable one.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many teams believe they are safe because backups run every night. An attacker who removes those backups takes that safety away. Sudden drops in backup success, or deleted snapshot records, are warnings you should treat as urgent. Recovering from a serious incident depends on copies the attacker could not reach.
howItWorks: The attacker reaches an account or system with rights over backups or virtual machines.
They delete stored recovery points, such as shadow copies or hypervisor snapshots.
Backup jobs or backup agents are stopped, or their storage is wiped or repointed.
Retention rules are shortened so old copies expire sooner than they should.
In cloud tenants, the same result comes from snapshot and vault settings.
Then encryption begins, and the organization has far less to restore from.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital that keeps spare generators in a locked room. An intruder does not touch the wards; they simply drain the fuel and cut the cables to the backup power. When the lights go out, the wards that looked fine become critical. Keeping a second generator somewhere else, and checking its fuel, is the difference between a short outage and a disaster.
takeaways: Treat backup deletion alerts as seriously as a confirmed intrusion.
Keep one copy that attackers cannot delete, even with admin rights.
Test your restore process before you need it in a real emergency.
